documents.title: Remove pkg_resources in favor of importlib.resources, etc.
documents.question: Why was pkg_resources removed?
documents.answer: The issue cites guidance discouraging pkg_resources in favor of importlib alternatives. It does not establish removal.

passages.title: Remove pkg_resources in favor of importlib.resources, etc.
passages.author: mgasner
passages.text:
As the docs for pkg_resources note:

```Use of pkg_resources is discouraged in favor of importlib.resources, importlib.metadata, and their backports (resources, metadata). Please consider using those libraries instead of pkg_resources.```

documents.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
documents.question: Why did Dagster replace FreshnessPolicy with freshness checks?
documents.answer: The guide describes confusing data-time calculations, alert fatigue, and automation behavior; checks provide customization using an existing concept.

passages.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
passages.author: dpeng817
passages.text:
As of 1.7, the `FreshnessPolicy` API has been deprecated in favor of two new asset check factories which check the freshness of passed-in assets. The following will serve as a guide to perform the necessary migration to the new APIs, as well as answer questions about why we’re making this change and what it entails.

1. A freshness policy on a time-window partitioned asset.

    If you have a freshness policy specified on a time-window partitioned asset, you should add a freshness check defined by the `build_time_partition_freshness_checks` API.

    This API functions differently than the original FreshnessPolicy API in a few ways.

    First, a time-window partitioned asset with a freshness policy was considered fresh if ALL completed partitions before the deadline have been materialized, whereas for a time partition freshness check, the asset is considered fresh if the most recent partition before the deadline has arrived, irrespective of earlier partitions.

    Second, the freshness policy API has two different parameters; a `cron_schedule`, which defines when we should start check for the existence of an asset; and `maximum_lag_minutes`, which defines the latest partition we should be searching for. For example, a `cron_schedule` of `"0 9 * * *"` and a `maximum_lag_minutes` of 540 would mean that we expect all partitions ending before midnight of the previous day are fresh. In contrast, the freshness check will derive which partition to search for from the cron schedule directly, instead of requiring a lag parameter to also be set. So, simply specifying a `cron_schedule` of `"0 9 * * *"` , the check will infer that the partition we expect is the one ending on midnight yesterday, since it’s the earliest partition to finish before 9am today.

    For the given invocation of a `FreshnessPolicy`, which expects a time-partitioned asset to be fresh by 9am daily:

    ```python
    @asset(
    	freshness_policy=FreshnessPolicy(cron_schedule="0 9 * * *", max_lag_minutes=540), 
    	partitions_def=DailyPartitionsDefinition(start_date="2021-01-01") 
    )
    def my_asset():
        ...
    ```

passages.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
passages.author: dpeng817
passages.text:
You could instead construct an asset and freshness check like so:

    ```python
    @asset(
    	partitions_def=DailyPartitionsDefinition(
    	  start_date=pendulum.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, tz="UTC")
      ) 
    )
    def my_asset():
        ...
        
    freshness_check = build_time_partition_freshness_checks(
      deadline_cron="0 9 * * *",
      assets=[my_asset],
    )
    ```

2. A freshness policy on a non-time-partitioned asset.

    We define a non-time-partitioned asset as one that either has no partitions, or has a partitions definition that does not derive from `TimeWindowPartitionsDefinition`. There are two different parameterizations possible for a non-time-partitioned asset.

    The first is to have a `freshness_cron` and a `maximum_lag_minutes` parameter both defined.

    ```python
    FreshnessPolicy(cron_schedule="0 9 * * *", maximum_lag_minutes=60)
    ```

    this is directly analogous to having a freshness check defined by the `build_last_update_freshness_checks` API, but the `lower_bound_delta` parameter replaces `maximum_lag_minutes`, and `deadline_cron` replaces `cron_schedule`.

    ```python
    import datetime
    
    freshness_checks = build_last_update_freshness(deadline_cron="0 9 * * *", lower_bound_delta=datetime.timedelta(minutes=60), assets=...)
    ```

    Second, you can have a `maximum_lag_minutes` parameterization only.

    ```python
    FreshnessPolicy(maximum_lag_minutes=60)
    ```

    which is directly analogous to only setting `lower_bound_delta` on the freshness check.

    ```python
    import datetime
    
    freshness_checks = build_last_update_freshness(lower_bound_delta=datetime.timedelta(minutes=60), assets=...)
    ```

passages.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
passages.author: dpeng817
passages.text:
F.A.Q.

- Why this change? Two reasons:
    - The previous way of computing “data time” for freshness was inflexible and confusing; while the new system allows users to override the data time of an asset more easily.
    - We felt that freshness as it currently exists was too heavyweight in the system. We found that the overdue status was leading to both alert fatigue and confusing automaterialization behavior. In contrast, composing freshness as asset checks allows us to take advantage of all the usability + customizability wins of asset checks (status alerts, custom UI, insights, etc) without needing to introduce a new concept to the system. In general, we want to reduce the number of “concepts” that users need to keep track of in order to have a production-ready dagster deployment, and reintroducing freshness as a type of check felt like an opportunity to do that.
- What happens to the overdue status populated by a freshness policy? The “overdue” status goes away. When an asset is evaluated to be overdue by a freshness check, it shows up as a failed asset check.
- What happens to freshness-based automaterialization? Freshness checks cannot currently be used in automaterialization rules. We are actively working on replacement to this behavior.
- When will I be forced to migrate off of FreshnessPolicy entirely? FreshnessPolicy will be entirely removed by 1.8. We will not remove it before a replacement is landed for freshness-based automaterialization.

passages.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
passages.author: emirkmo
passages.text:
> We will not remove it before a replacement is landed for freshness-based automaterialization.

As we have been using freshness based automation since at least 1.2 (reconciliation sensors), I highly support this part, since automation is one of the two primary benefits of freshness. The second being Freshness based observability, which has been a big component of the benefit of Dagster's UI for our stakeholders. Without seeing the freshness status at a glance nor being able to schedule based off it, it would be a big downgrade.

Mainly, Freshness Policy allows a declarative mapping from a data contract, i.e. some promise about asset freshness written in code and version control, to its scheduling and details on the asset page. So apart from automation, the bigger aspect is solving this translation from data contract to the scheduling and asset overview for data assets, which was quite natural with the freshness policy. (Think about FreshnessPolicy from a grab bag of dbt and python assets from multiple code locations, being translated and effortlessly scheduling themselves, while providing an overview of asset freshness and status at a glass. That is what FreshnessPolicy and automation based on it has easily allowed. This functionality would be excellent to carry forward or improve).

The functionality of Freshness based checks could already be created based on the Freshness Policy, even before the explicit introduction of freshness checks (or even asset checks to be fair). The "check" seem like a side functionality compared to the above uses of automated scheduling and observability.

I would request that the big picture view of freshness as a promise made by the asset be maintained with the new implementation. It should ideally be easy to assign and use this information for scheduling and in the UI, as this the key metric for most assets when building up observability. Checks on data quality are secondary to the data being there or not.

(Completely agree the FreshnessPolicy was opaque and hard to grasp. Glad to see a rework, but worried about wholesale tossing out without having some of the core functionality.)

passages.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
passages.author: OwenKephart
passages.locator: Comment 2 of 2, reply to comment 1 (part 1 of 3)
passages.text:
Hi @emirkmo, thank you for providing this feedback! I’d like to focus on your points regarding the integration of freshness with scheduling, as this is something that (as you note) we’ve been pretty vague about.

TLDR: We are deprecating the current notion of freshness scheduling as it had deep problems. However we are committed to supporting lazy/on-demand scheduling, but will do so in the context a new system. We don’t have exact timing on when the discussed changes will land, but this is the focus of active development.

To frame the issue, I want to break down the current freshness-based scheduling system into the things that work well conceptually, and the things that don’t (from our perspective). At a high level, we want to double down on the useful things and get rid of things that are confusing or actively bad.

What’s good:

- Deferring scheduling decisions to children
    - In many cases, an asset in the middle of the graph does not actually have an opinion on how often it should be executed. It exists to service downstream assets, and so setting an explicit policy (run once a day) is redundant and error prone (as you might later decide that the downstream asset needs to run once every hour, which would require you to manually update all upstream assets with this new frequency).
    - Freshness-based scheduling handles this nicely, as “lazy” assets can adapt to downstream freshness policies
- Connecting expectations about an asset to actions taken on that asset
    - As you bring up in your post, it’s nice to have a contract that can be “self-enforcing”, i.e. the system automatically makes decisions in such a way to abide by the provided limit.

passages.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
passages.author: OwenKephart
passages.locator: Comment 2 of 2, reply to comment 1 (part 2 of 3)
passages.text:
What’s not so good:

- Global, unconfigurable definition of “data time”
    - FreshnessPolicies work off of a global view of the asset graph. Beyond being slow and expensive to calculate, it’s also quite common for this to result in incorrect answers. If a single upstream node in the graph is expected to update just once in awhile, it’s quite challenging to work around this. The AssetCheck based system is more customizable in this regard.
- SLA-based scheduling is hard to define precisely
    - In most cases, there are multiple ways to approach hitting a data freshness SLA, depending on the specific weights you place on minimizing redundant work vs. minimizing risk of missing that SLA. You don’t have any way of precisely predicting exactly how long materializing some set of assets would take, and so the precise time you decide to start your computation is more of an art than a science. This means we need to support some level of customizability at this level, which the existing system does not.
- Understandability / observability / composability
    - The existing freshness-based scheduling system makes decisions in an entirely parallel way from other auto-materialize rules. This means that there is no way to link its outputs (runs) to the complicated system of inputs it used to produce that output decision. This also makes it hard to compose these scheduling decisions with other parts of the system. I.e. you’d struggle to implement something along the lines of “freshness-based scheduling, but with a maximum rate limit”.

Outline of a Plan

As background, we have been moving towards a world in which all scheduling decisions are expressed as an arbitrary boolean expression of conditions, i.e. “(I haven’t been materialized since 8am) & (all of my parents have been materialized since 8am)”. The term for this would be a SchedulingCondition, so you can build up expressions such as:

```python
~SchedulingCondition.updated_since_cron("...")
& SchedulingCondition.all_deps_match(
    SchedulingCondition.updated_since_cron("...")
)
```

Note: This is a successor to AutoMaterializePolicy, and backwards compatibility will be maintained in the short term. SchedulingConditions can be seen as implementing a superset of the capabilities of AutoMaterializeRules.

passages.title: Freshness Policy -> Freshness Checks migration guide
passages.author: OwenKephart
passages.locator: Comment 2 of 2, reply to comment 1 (part 3 of 3)
passages.text:
The above expression would (roughly) result in an asset being materialized on a given schedule, waiting for its parents to finish before proceeding. For convenience, this sort of “composite condition” would be available through a static constructor, along the lines of `SchedulingCondition.on_cron("...")`.

To tackle the issue of “lazy” scheduling (i.e. assets that only exist for the purpose of satisfying downstream requirements), we plan on introducing a condition that represents a union of all child conditions. This allows you to set an asset’s scheduling condition to something like `SchedulingCondition.child_condition()`, which would defer all scheduling logic to the downstream asset (and this would work recursively, meaning the asset could look arbitrarily far down the graph to find the “source” policy):

[image: Screenshot 2024-05-09 at 2 13 13 PM]

This means that, for any asset with an explicit “freshness policy”, it can be left up to the user to define how that policy would be best satisfied. In most cases, this would probably be a simple cron schedule condition (such as the one described above), which matches the cadence of your freshness policy. To avoid forcing this information to be double-encoded in both the freshness check and the scheduling policy, we can provide a `SchedulingCondition.infer_from_freshness_checks()` , which would create a condition that is designed to keep the asset in line with its expressed freshness goal. However, the user could at any point customize this policy to better suit their needs.

Once again, we appreciate your feedback, and if you have thoughts on this direction we’re more than happy to hear them! We’d love to talk more with you about this, either on this issue or via Slack / email.

documents.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
documents.question: Why did Dagster move toward Pipes instead of continuing with Step Launchers?
documents.answer: The announcement identifies coupling, deployment complexity, remote dependencies, and customization constraints. Pipes favors modular remote execution with more user responsibility.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: danielgafni
passages.text:
# StepLauncher supersession announcement

# TLDR

The StepLauncher (https://docs.dagster.io/_apidocs/internals#step-launchers-experimental) is being superseded with Dagster Pipes (https://docs.dagster.io/concepts/dagster-pipes). We recommend users start exploring Dagster Pipes and consider migrating (see the Spark example (https://docs.dagster.io/guides/migrations/from-step-launchers-to-pipes#migrating-from-spark-step-launchers-to-dagster-pipes)) existing `StepLauncher` usages to Pipes. While `StepLauncher` will remain available, this feature will no longer be receiving active development.

Users who prefer Step Launchers to Pipes because of some features like `IOManager` integration are welcome to do so, given they accept the increased development and deployment complexity.

# Context

`StepLauncher` was an experimental Dagster resource which could be used to run Dagster steps in remote environments such as Spark. The following step launchers were implemented:

- `dagster_databricks.databricks_pyspark_step_launcher`
- `dagster_aws.emr.emr_pyspark_step_launcher`

The goal of step launchers was to seamlessly execute Dagster code in Spark or another remote environment. In particular, a `StepLauncher` is responsible for:

1. Setting up the remote environment - uploading Dagster code and installing dependencies
2. Executing the `op/asset` remotely
3. Fetching logs and Dagster events from the remote process and making them available to Dagster.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: danielgafni
passages.text:
However, this power came at the cost of significant implementation complexity and feature coupling. If you've been using step launchers, especially in Spark, you might wonder why we're moving away from this approach. Historically, we tried to integrate business logic and orchestration in external runtimes like Spark using framework-level abstractions. While `StepLauncher` aimed to make remote execution easier, it faced several challenges that made adoption difficult:

- Rigid Code Structure: You had to structure your deployed code around Dagster code locations and definitions, which could be impractical if you had existing Spark jobs or dependency conflicts.
- Deployment Limitations: `StepLauncher` managed code deployment at runtime, which often conflicted with DevOps processes. Many users preferred managing deployments during push time instead.
- Complex Customization: Writing custom step launchers was complex, making them difficult to extend and use effectively.
- Runtime dependencies: The `StepLauncher` required to have `dagster` installed in the remote environment, which might introduce version conflicts or increase the complexity of the deployment process.
- Usage with other programming languages: because of the previous point, it was not possible to use `StepLauncher` with programming languages other than Python, which is a blocker for popular Scala/Java Spark workloads.

For those who do not want to structure their Spark business logic around Dagster definitions, we believe that Dagster Pipes -- a more composable and lightweight solution -- is the right path forward.

# Dagster Pipes

Dagster Pipes is a wire protocol that handles parameter/context passing to the remote process, and log/metadata gathering from the remote process. This approach aligns better with Dagster's philosophy of modularity and extensibility, enabling users to create more flexible and powerful remote execution solutions, albeit with some additional setup responsibility.

Some of the improvements over `StepLauncher` are:

➕ Increased composability: Pipes components can be mixed and matched, allowing for use in a wide variety of environments.

➕ Decreased complexity: individual Pipes components can be implemented and tested in isolation, making it easier to develop and maintain custom solutions. This modular approach allows for greater flexibility and adaptability to specific use cases.

➕ Improved extensibility: Users can easily extend the existing existing family of Pipes components to meet their unique requirements, fostering a more diverse ecosystem of integrations.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: danielgafni
passages.text:
➕ Lightweight: Pipes can execute unmodified scripts. In order to send additional Dagster events (such as Dagster metadata or asset check results) back to the orchestration process, a zero-dependency (and single-file) `dagster-pipes` Python package can be installed in the remote environment.

➕ Language-agnostic: Implementing Dagster Pipes in additional programming languages is very tractable. Dagster customers have already done this. Right now we only have an official implementation for Python, but we will be adding support to more languages in the near future (JVM languages being in progress).

As Pipes are more lightweight and give you greater control, they also come with some responsibilities:

➖ Pipes do not automatically set up the remote environment. This responsibility now falls to the user, typically handled through CI/CD processes.

➖ Pipes to not automatically execute `op/asset` body. Instead, the users are typically expected to provide an external script which will be launched by Pipes.

# Pipes Clients

We have implemented a set of opinionated Pipes clients on top of the Pipes framework for some popular services.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: dinis-rodrigues
passages.text:
This will imply major major breaking changes in the future. From the release notes the step launcher:
>will not be removed from the codebase until Dagster 2.0 is released

Meaning that from v2 support it could be removed entirely.
Organizations currently using step launchers and io_managers (like us) will need to refactor the entire codebase to work with dagster pipes.

Yes the step launcher has its drawbacks, but it is easily customizable (like dagster pipes), by extending its class in my opinion.
If we compare the two, the boiler plate code which is needed to setup dagster pipes, rounds up to the same as a custom inherited step launcher.

And the biggest drawback of them all is the deprecation of io_manager with dagster pipes. For example, many spark jobs rely on intermediate outputs (instead of cache) to optimize the spark job. We for example, have intermediate outputs in all jobs, because we have complex queries which require this optimization.

Having to configure each op with a hardcoded "io_manager" in the end / beginning, just to make things work, is just friction to developers.

I think the idea behind dagster pipes is good, but it feels like we had a battletested steplauncher and now we are "obligated" to use a new less-featured almost blank canvas tool. For newcomers in dagster, this might be okay, but for existing users, its a barrier.

If the step launcher had its flaws, it should've been a matter of improving the existing solution, instead of building from the ground up a new one and making existing workflows deprecated.

Maybe this opinion is due to my lack of experience and experimentation with pipes, but just the thought of having to refactor everything, makes me demotivated just to try it

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: danielgafni
passages.text:
Hey!

Thank you for the feedback, that's exactly why this discussion was created.

> will not be removed from the codebase until Dagster 2.0 is released

This wording was poor, I'll make sure to change it. Two points here:

1. We don't have any timeline or plans for Dagster 2.0. This means this can be considered as a very distant point in time.
2. Actually, we aren't aiming to remove Step Launchers even in 2.0. There are no reasons for doing this. So you could keep using them as long as you'd like to. After all, they are just normal resources (just like Pipes) and aren't dependent on any specific framework features. We are planning to stop active development of Step Launchers, but they aren't going anywhere.

> Having to configure each op with a hardcoded "io_manager" in the end / beginning, just to make things work, is just friction to developers.

I very much agree with that. I'll let @schrockn elaborate

CC @yuhan feedback above ^^

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: schrockn
passages.text:
@dinis-rodrigues thanks for the feedback.

For people like yourselves who are "all in" on step launchers to the point of building their own step launchers, our recommendation is not to port to Pipes. It is working for you now. For people who are willing commit to step launchers and to have it own deployment, install dagster in the remote environment, etc, step launchers provide more features. We will clarify the wording of the discussion on this point.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: dinis-rodrigues
passages.text:
Let me just clarify that I'm all for it on the new dagster-pipes features. I would love to see those same features on step launchers without losing the io_manager, for example.

We extended the functionality of the existing step launchers to achieve some extra/custom functionality.
We are all-in on step launchers because we have been all-in on dagster from the beginning. Step launchers were what was available, and we just built from that.

We've been closely following the new features, and I just raised this awareness because of possible major refactoring.
In the near future we want and will use/extend dagster-pipes. But with the io_manager "issue", it's not feasible at the moment.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: jmccartin
passages.text:
Hi, just come across this discussion after a ticket I was watching was closed, and this was referenced.

We are in the same boat as @dinis-rodrigues, our company makes use of remote execution on Azure Databricks quite heavily, with a somewhat complex chain of custom IO managers to handle data loading and writes. I haven't looked too deeply into dagster-pipes, but from the sounds of it, our codebase would be very difficult to port over. I would be fine continuing to use the current step launchers, but there is some long-term concern regarding the Databricks SDK (the existing step launcher is built on a deprecated SDK version). If there is no longer going to be active development from the core team, would it be up to the community to take over? It would be good to get an idea of how many people/teams are affected by this.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: danielgafni
passages.text:
1. re: switching to Pipes in your case - you are right about it probably being too complicated right now. I suggest you stay on Step Launchers. Perhaps in the future Pipes could become more compatible with IOManagers which will make it easier for you to switch.
2. re: community taking over `StepLauncher` support - potentially, I don't see serious obstacles to that, but it's better if @yuhan or @schrockn could answer to this question

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: jmccartin
passages.text:
Any update on this? I notice that the documentation for the step launcher is essentially now removed (https://docs.dagster.io/api/python-api/libraries/dagster-databricks#step-launcher), and the line "usage is discouraged" seems to conflict with what you guys are saying here.

Should I just create a fork of the library and see how far I get with regards to updating it for the new SDK version?

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: danielgafni
passages.text:
Hey @jmccartin!

We've updated the wording here (https://github.com/dagster-io/dagster/pull/27508). It should be aligned with this thread now.

As for your other question:

> If there is no longer going to be active development from the core team, would it be up to the community to take over?

 let's see if maybe @cmpadden @yuhan have an answer?

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: schrockn
passages.text:
Just to expand on this, @jmccartin thanks for the feedback here and as @danielgafni we've updated the docs to clarify the state of things.

To provide additional context and framing, Pipes is a "one step backwards two step forwards" type of situation. Pipes actually has _less_ features than step launchers when it comes to executing on systems like Spark. But Pipes is easier to use, more composable, and more architecturally sound. For most people step launchers were just too hard to use and customize, and step launchers were too presumptuous about taking over responsibility for deploying code.

Our plan moving forward to build features that stack on top of Pipes to allow users to separate I/O and compute in the same way that I/O managers do today (and would likely be backwards compatible with I/O managers). We think this approach would be more flexible and composable: E.g. you could be able to deploy the transforms to a remote cluster without having to bring in _all_ of dagster.

Until we have such a capability we will not eliminate or abandon Step Launchers. New users have much more success with Pipes so we are driving them towards that, hence the messaging. If you are one of the intrepid souls that have successfully bought into step launchers, it's quite a magical experience, and we don't want to take that away. We look forward to bringing similar capabilities to a broader audience in the future.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: jtv8
passages.text:
Weighing in here as someone who evaluated both Pipes and Step Launchers and purposely chose Step Launchers: the Pipes experience is the _exact opposite_ of what I want.

- It requires you to split your asset definitions into two Python files in two separate locations, one with your metadata and dependencies and the other with your actual asset code. The fact that you _don't_ normally have to do this is one of the key selling points of Dagster.
- You can't locally test your code as a single artefact in the same way you could with `no_step_launcher`.
- It does not deploy your code for you and requires you to develop a whole additional CI/CD process to push your code to Databricks (I disagree with the argument that this is a deployment activity, any more than you "deploy" SQL to a database when you execute it).
- It requires you to wrap your code in boilerplate just to do simple things like read parameters and report asset materializations, rather than doing what Dagster is good at: leveraging simple Python functions.
- It does not appear to support I/O managers at all - these are perhaps the most useful feature in Dagster for platform teams who want to create abstractions to standardise how assets are read and written.

In summary: What I _really_ want is a way to write Spark assets as simple Python functions, and I want to do it in a way that's completely agnostic of the execution environment - as an asset developer, most of the time, I don't want to handle low-level code for configuring and communicating with that execution environment. Those are concerns for platform developers. Until it's possible to use Pipes in such a way, I can't see myself recommending it.

If anything, it would be preferable to go in completely the _opposite_ direction and implement a fully fledged run launcher for environments like Databricks and cut out the Kubernetes job entirely, if such a thing were possible. But absent that, I'll continue to use Step Launchers for as long as they're supported - and if we were forced to use Pipes in the future, we would probably end up building our own abstractions that make them work exactly how Step Launchers do now.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: schrockn
passages.text:
Hey @jtv8 thanks for the thoughtful commentary. We understand completely that for people who are fully bought into that entire stack, Step Launchers provided a pretty compelling end-to-end product experience.

For Spark and Databricks specifically we are _very_ excited about Spark/Databricks connect and are very actively looking at working on this. We have customers that already use it to great effect.

With Connect, we think we will be able to provide a true best-of-both-worlds experience, allowing you to keep your business logic in Dagster but do actual execution on remote clusters without having to manage deployment at all. Step Launchers are completely unnecessary in that world, but you get the lightweight functional API you desire.

My recommendation for you is the following: continue using step launchers and i/o managers since you are getting value out of them. As our Connect integration matures, you should be able to move that quite easily and eliminate step launchers entirely, which is a more robust approach the leverages more of the built-in capabilities in Spark/Databricks.

passages.title: Step Launchers supersession announcement
passages.author: jtv8
passages.text:
Hi @schrockn - thanks for sharing that! Leveraging Databricks Connect would make perfect sense - it would separate concerns properly between Dagster as an orchestrator and Databricks as a compute environment, and would provide a consistent experience whether the code is running in Dagster or a local development environment. Also, I suspect it would improve cluster spin-up times quite a bit, which is always a big pain point with Databricks.

I'll recommend to my team that you we do what you suggested, and I'll keep an eye out for the Databricks Connect integration!
